title: 5 Mental Models That Will Take Your Leadership from Good to Great
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain argues that what separates good leaders from great ones is how they think, and offers five mental models as cognitive tools for decision-making under pressure. First principles thinking strips a problem to its fundamental elements, illustrated with Elon Musk's questioning of rocket costs and a team repeatedly missing deadlines. Inversion asks how to avoid failure rather than how to succeed, drawing on Charlie Munger. The map is not the territory warns leaders that any plan is only an approximation of reality and must be revised as conditions change, a point Jain makes partly through his own compulsive planning. Occam's Razor counsels simplicity against decision fatigue, illustrated with an over-engineered property spreadsheet, and the Pareto Principle directs effort to the vital few activities, clients and performers. Each model is paired with an application example and self-check questions, and the piece ends with a reading list of books, articles and podcasts.
points: Jain locates the difference between good and great leaders in their thinking tools rather than their activity, positioning mental models as ways to cut through complexity.
First principles thinking is applied to inherited team processes: break them into steps and ask what each step is actually for.
Inversion turns planning toward failure modes, for example listing what would make a product launch fail and mitigating each.
The map-is-not-the-territory model is used to warn against clinging to strategies that worked before, illustrated by the author's own over-attachment to plans.
Occam's Razor and the Pareto Principle are paired as remedies for decision fatigue and diffuse effort, focusing leaders on the simplest route and the vital 20 percent.
quotes: So, the key differentiator between good leaders and great leaders is how they think. That’s where mental models come in. Mental models are powerful tools that leaders can use to shape how they approach problems, and make decisions.

As a leader, if you adopt first principles thinking it can give you a fresh perspective and uncover solutions that you may otherwise never discover. By focusing on the most fundamental truths of a problem, you eliminate unnecessary complexity and get to the root of the issue. This allows you to focus on more creative and innovation approaches to solving problems.

This mental model forces you to look at problems from a different angle, helping you identify risks and prevent mistakes before they happen. Charlie Munger is a big advocate of this model. He often says, “All I want to know is where I’m going to die, so I’ll never go there.

This mental model highlights the gap between your perception (the map) and reality (the territory). It reminds leaders that no matter how well-planned your strategy is, it’s only an approximation of reality.
It’s easy to get caught in the weeds as a leader, trying to consider every possible angle before making a call. But sometimes, the simplest solution is the best. That’s where Occam’s Razor comes in.

The Pareto Principle states that 80% of outcomes come from 20% of efforts. In leadership, this means that only a handful of your actions — your “vital few” — create the biggest impact, while the rest may be just noise.
Great leaders use mental models to guide their decisions. They use these models to reduce complexity and to make effective decisions.
